changes.old: ## Почему сервис нужно проверять под нагрузкой
changes.new: ### Blocked measurements and individual-call latency Suppose an operation takes 2 microseconds, while starting and stopping the timer adds 12 microseconds per measured interval. Timing one call would report 14 microseconds. Timing 1000 consecutive calls would report 2012 microseconds in total, or 2.012 microseconds per call. These are assumed costs, not measurements of Python or CUDA. For a fixed per-block overhead $h$, a block of $n$ calls of duration $t$ has an amortized time $$ \frac{nt+h}{n}=t+\frac{h}{n}. $$ A larger block reduces the overhead per call, but leaves fewer separately timed blocks within a fixed measurement budget. PyTorch's [Benchmark recipe, section 4](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/recipes/recipes/benchmark.html#benchmarking-with-blocked-autorange) describes how it chooses and repeats the blocks. The complete explanatory paragraph is retained in its original language: > While `timeit.Timer.autorange` takes a single continuous measurement > of at least 0.2 seconds, `torch.utils.benchmark.Timer.blocked_autorange` > takes many measurements whose times total at least 0.2 seconds (which > can be changed by the `min_run_time` parameter) subject to the constraint > that timing overhead is a small fraction of the overall measurement. > This is accomplished by first running with an increasing number of runs > per loop until the runtime is much larger than measurement overhead > (which also serves as a warm up), and then taking measurements until > the target time is reached. This has the useful properties that it wastes > less data and allows us to compute statistics to estimate the reliability > of the measurements. *PyTorch contributors, [pinned recipe source](https://github.com/pytorch/tutorials/blob/5672cd98a7671eda4d9122b10f8eec580f74d03e/recipes_source/recipes/benchmark.py#L294-L305), [BSD 3-Clause, complete notice](/licenses/pytorch-tutorials-5672cd98-BSD-3-Clause.txt). Wording unchanged; reStructuredText inline-code delimiters converted to Markdown.* In the pinned [Timer implementation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/5c4886908584029761b579af026dcfb627c84070/torch/utils/benchmark/utils/timer.py#L303-L382), calibration selects a block size before collecting the returned samples. The collection loop adds whole-block durations until their sum reaches `min_run_time`. Calibration and other setup add elapsed time outside that sum; the argument is not an upper bound on the duration of the Python call. A long block can also leave only one returned measurement. More calls inside that block do not create more independently timed observations. The returned `Measurement` keeps those block totals in `raw_times`, in seconds, and the common block size in `number_per_run`. Its `times` property divides each total by that count. Median and IQR are then calculated across the normalized block times. They describe variability between amortized timings, not the distribution of the individual calls inside a block. The [Measurement source](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/5c4886908584029761b579af026dcfb627c84070/torch/utils/benchmark/utils/common.py#L75-L190) makes that division explicit. Two different call sequences can produce exactly the same block totals. Consider ten blocks of 100 calls each: | Assumed calls within each block | Block total | Mean per call | |---|---:|---:| | 100 calls at 10 ms | 1000 ms | 10 ms | | 98 calls at 1 ms, two at 451 ms | 1000 ms | 10 ms | Both sequences produce ten normalized observations of 10 ms. Yet their individual-call nearest-rank p99 values are 10 ms and 451 ms respectively: in the second sequence, 20 of the 1000 calls take 451 ms. Once only the block totals remain, there is no way to determine which sequence occurred. The following deterministic example constructs actual PyTorch measurement objects from these assumed totals. It does not run a timed operation. `TaskSpec` is an internal metadata type from the pinned implementation, used here to inspect the stored representation. Application benchmarks normally obtain `Measurement` objects from `Timer` instead of constructing this metadata themselves. ~~~python from math import ceil from torch.utils.benchmark import Measurement from torch.utils.benchmark.utils.common import TaskSpec def nearest_rank(values, probability): if not values or not 0 < probability <= 1: raise ValueError("nonempty sample and probability in (0, 1] required") return sorted(values)[ceil(probability * len(values)) - 1] def group_measurement(groups): if not groups or not groups[0]: raise ValueError("nonempty groups required") number = len(groups[0]) if any(len(group) != number for group in groups): raise ValueError("fixed number_per_run required") # Inputs are assumed individual-call durations in milliseconds. return Measurement( number_per_run=number, raw_times=[sum(group) / 1000 for group in groups], task_spec=TaskSpec(stmt="assumed_call()", setup="pass", num_threads=1), ) uniform = [[10] * 100 for _ in range(10)] bursty = [[1] * 98 + [451, 451] for _ in range(10)] uniform_measurement = group_measurement(uniform) bursty_measurement = group_measurement(bursty) assert uniform_measurement.raw_times == bursty_measurement.raw_times == [1.] * 10 assert uniform_measurement.times == bursty_measurement.times == [.01] * 10 assert uniform_measurement.iqr == bursty_measurement.iqr == 0 assert uniform_measurement.meets_confidence(.1) assert bursty_measurement.meets_confidence(.1) uniform_calls = [t for group in uniform for t in group] bursty_calls = [t for group in bursty for t in group] assert nearest_rank(uniform_calls, .99) == 10 assert nearest_rank(bursty_calls, .99) == 451 assert nearest_rank(uniform_measurement.times, .99) * 1000 == 10 assert nearest_rank(bursty_measurement.times, .99) * 1000 == 10 assert sum(t > 50 for t in bursty_calls) == 20 print("individual-call p99, ms:", 10, 451) print("normalized-block p99, ms:", 10, 10) ~~~ The zero IQR follows from the identical block means. In this pinned implementation, `meets_confidence` checks `IQR / median < threshold`; the method's name does not establish a confidence level for an individual-call p99. `adaptive_autorange` uses that spread criterion along with runtime and sample-count conditions. It cannot reconstruct the durations discarded by block averaging. For a microbenchmark, retain `number_per_run`, the number of returned blocks and their times so another reader can interpret the reported median. For request-tail latency, record each request's arrival and completion under the intended load, including the errors and timeouts. Increasing the timer's repetition count cannot recover observations that were never recorded. ## Почему сервис нужно проверять под нагрузкой
